meta.title: Who really said "Tell 'em what you're going to tell 'em; next, tell 'em; next, tell 'em what you told 'em"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Aristotle never said it. The earliest documented version is a 1908 English newspaper crediting an unnamed preacher. It's an early-1900s pulpit maxim.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Tell 'em what you're going to tell 'em; next, tell 'em; next, tell 'em what you told 'em'?
meta.ogDescription: No — Aristotle never said it. The earliest documented version is a 1908 English newspaper crediting an unnamed preacher, not the ancient philosopher.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — an early-1900s pulpit maxim
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Aristotle said or wrote this. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest strong match appeared in 1908 in the Northern Daily Mail of Durham, England, ascribed to an unnamed veteran preacher — a folk maxim of oratory that was only later pinned on Aristotle (and on Dale Carnegie). Aristotle’s Rhetoric discusses beginnings, middles and ends and recommends repetition in the epilogue, but never this three-part ‘tell ’em’ template.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

An unnamed veteran preacher (reported via J. H. Jowett)
Misattributed to Aristotle; anonymous modern origin

source.excerpt: In the first part I tell ’em what I am going to tell ’em; in the second part — well, I tell ’em; in the third part I tell ’em what I’ve told ’em.
trail: The authoritative investigation by Quote Investigator dates the earliest strong match to 1908 in the Northern Daily Mail, crediting an unnamed preacher — not Aristotle.
QI notes the saying circulated among religious orators for decades and was later credited to figures including Dale Carnegie, none of whom originated it.
Aristotle’s actual Rhetoric recommends stating your subject and summarizing in the epilogue, but as QI observes, that is not the tripartite ‘tell ’em’ formula of the quotation.
source.excerptNote: The 1908 wording as quoted by Quote Investigator, attributed to an anonymous preacher — the earliest known form of the saying.

source.rightsNote: The wording is an anonymous English-language folk maxim of oratory whose earliest documented appearance is a 1908 newspaper — well before 1931 and with no identifiable individual author — so the phrase itself is in the public domain. It is not a work of Aristotle’s.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Why it lands on Aristotle
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Ancient Greek philosopher · founder of formal rhetoric & logic
author.bio: Aristotle of Stagira did more than anyone to systematize the art of persuasion — his Rhetoric is the foundational treatise on how speeches are built, and he did stress clear openings, summarizing epilogues, and useful repetition. That real association makes him a magnet for any snappy ‘rules of speaking’ line, which is likely how this catchy but modern pulpit maxim drifted onto his name centuries later. He never used the three-part ‘tell ’em’ formula.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s classic ‘sounds ancient, isn’t’ quotes — a modern speaking maxim dressed up in a toga.

items.why: Endlessly shared as ancient wisdom, but Quote Investigator finds no basis for it in Aristotle’s works; his Rhetoric uses different structures and never states this three-part formula.
Also frequently named, but QI lists Carnegie among the many later figures the saying attached to, not its originator.
The earliest strong match, from the 1908 Northern Daily Mail, credits an unnamed veteran preacher — the maxim grew out of early-1900s religious oratory, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: No single author owns it: it is an anonymous early-20th-century maxim of oratory, first documented in 1908 and only later mis-credited to Aristotle, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line survives because it is a genuinely useful teaching device — a memorable rule of thumb for structuring any talk, sermon, or presentation. Attaching it to Aristotle, the father of rhetoric, gives a modern classroom mnemonic the authority of antiquity.

That is exactly the pattern behind most fake Aristotle quotes: a real association (he did write the foundational work on speech structure) makes him a plausible-sounding home for lines he never actually wrote.
context.pull: A modern speaking maxim in ancient dress — first seen in a 1908 newspaper, not in Aristotle.
